title: Rome has not defined the dispute; Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists, Innocent X and Alexander VII the other side
source_text: XXXV. Porro cum lis ista apud Romanos Pontifices, & coetum Cardinalium ad hoc deputatorum saepe fuerit mota & agitata, hactenus tamen illam nondum definierunt, & licitum suis esse voluerunt hanc aut illam sententiam pro arbitrio tenere & tueri. Quanquam sicut sub hujus saeculi initium & praecedentis finem Thomistarum sententiae favere visi sunt Romani Pontifices Paulus V. & Clemens VIII. Sic postremis hisce annis oppositae doctrinae magis favisse videntur eorum successores Innocentius X. & Alexander VII. Unde factum est ut jam in Schola Romana longe communior evaserit, & a maxima parte Theologorum teneatur.
pass_a_gloss: Further although that dispute has often been moved and agitated before the Roman Pontiffs, and a body of Cardinals deputed for this, yet hitherto they have not yet defined it, and have willed it to be lawful for their people to hold and defend this or that opinion at their choice. Although as about the beginning of this century and the end of the preceding the Roman Pontiffs Paul V. and Clement VIII. seemed to favour the opinion of the Thomists. So in these last years their successors Innocent X. and Alexander VII. seem to have favoured the opposite doctrine more. Whence it has come about that it has now become far more common in the Roman School, and is held by the greatest part of the Theologians.
pass_b_english: The dispute has often been raised and argued before the popes of Rome and before a body of cardinals appointed for the purpose, yet so far they have not settled it, and they have allowed their people to hold and defend either view as they choose.

Around the turn of this century, at the close of the last, Popes Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists' view. In these last years their successors Innocent X and Alexander VII seem to have leaned rather toward the opposite teaching. As a result it has now become by far the more common view in the Roman School and is held by most of its theologians.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
